accuracy.evidence: Definition matches the PSHE Association KS2 programme of study (stereotypes based on sex, gender, race, religion, age and disability can be unfair, negative or destructive) and the IB PYP PSPE identity strand. The score data mirror Hyde et al. (2008, Science): over seven million US pupils in grades 2 to 11 showed no meaningful gender gap in maths, so the lab's 0.2-point gap with wide spread is faithful.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known slips: a stereotype is fine if it fits some people (the 6 of 12 flip count), compliments cannot be stereotypes (glasses and kinder girls cards), a fact about one person is a stereotype (Ayo, grandma), off-point counter-examples (Nan Rose loves knitting, some boys like maths), and answering with insults or silence.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagstereo combines a flip-card grid with a running fit/does-not-fit tally, a drag-to-break claim box that only accepts the matching counter-example, a two-row dot plot that a slider merges into one interleaved line with hidden-identity dots, and drag-a-reply speech scenes. No other lab models group variation; the shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea comes from acting: flipping all twelve cards shows the label is wrong for half; dropping the wrong person gives a reason it cannot break that claim; merging the rows and revealing three grey dots shows a score cannot predict a group; replies are judged on calmness plus a counter-example, with a reason for each wrong reply.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: All 12 boys love football, Girls and boys split apart when lined up by score, and No it is a compliment for the glasses claim. The task right after each one tests the guess and the done message says whether it held, naming the predicted option.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with tagged wrong answers, each explained: a fact about one person versus a group, off-point counter-example (Some boys like maths), the compliment stereotype (All Asian kids are good at maths), between-group versus within-group spread, and insulting or giving up when Kai says ballet is for girls. Correct position rotates each round.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores FK 3.4 against the learner limit of 6.5 with short sentences and a named child in every example. Adult text scores FK 5.2 against 9.5 and uses the curriculum terms stereotype, individual differences, counter-example, identity, stereotype threat and the KS2 protected characteristics list.

no_filler.evidence: No stock phrases; the filler gate passed. Kid paragraphs each give one idea and a concrete example; adult paragraphs give curriculum placement, the research on variation, the four common mistakes and what the lab does. The explanation overlaps other lessons by under 12%.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark show a three-column 12-card grid, two-column person cards, a full-width slider ball and eight list rows that clear the counter label. Pointer tests on the iPhone viewport flipped all twelve cards, dragged Leo, Ray and Amira onto claims, merged the line and revealed dots, and dragged a reply.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs axe run found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme on desktop or iPhone. Every canvas action has a labelled button: flip next card, one per person, mix into one line and reveal top dot, one per sentence and one per reply. The canvas aria-label reads every result aloud.
